title: Jewish Renewal
hookLine: Zalman Schachter-Shalomi joined Hasidic spirituality with egalitarian openness

cards: The chairs are in a circle, not rows. Someone starts a melody with no words, just a sound, and it goes around once, twice, ten times, until the whole room is carrying it. A woman leads the next prayer.
A man near the window sways with his eyes closed. Then the room drops into a long silence before the Hebrew begins again.

Some of this would be at home in a Hasidic study house; some would surprise the people praying there. The rabbi whose life made rooms like this possible was Zalman Schachter-Shalomi, called Reb Zalman by his students.

teach.b: Reb Zalman was formed in Hasidism, in the Chabad world, where prayer is meant to be felt as well as said: the wordless melody called a niggun, the joy, the long gathering around a rebbe's table.
The Psalm says it plainly: "Serve the LORD with gladness: come before his presence with singing." Then the opening.

teach.h: WOMEN AND MEN LEAD SIDE BY SIDE.
teach.b: He carried that warmth to people who would never have walked into a Hasidic synagogue, and in Renewal communities women and men lead prayer, teach and serve as rabbis side by side. Now the forms.
Renewal gatherings may chant one line again and again until it settles, sit in silent meditation, move, sing in Hebrew and English, and pray with the body as well as the book.
Reb Zalman cared about the craft of prayer the way a musician cares about practice: how to make the words land in a living person. Finally, the name.

teach.h: RENEW OUR DAYS AS OF OLD.
teach.b: In the traditional service, as the Torah scroll goes back into the ark, the congregation sings a verse from Lamentations: "renew our days as of old."

Renewal in that verse is not novelty. It is going back to a source to find it fresh. Other Jews ask real questions in return: how far new forms can stretch, and how binding halakha remains inside them.
Renewal Jews hold a range of answers on that, too. The same verse is sung in Renewal circles and in Hasidic study houses, and each reads it in its own way.

how: Jewish Renewal communities pray with chanting, wordless melodies, silence and movement alongside the traditional Hebrew service, and women and men lead prayer and serve as rabbis equally.

games.q: you're Reb Zalman. you love the joy of Hasidic prayer, and you meet people who have never felt it. what do you do?
o: keep it inside the Hasidic world.
carry its warmth to everyone, with women and men leading equally.
drop prayer and teach only ideas.
games.why: he opened Hasidic warmth and prayer craft to people of every background, and in Renewal women and men lead side by side.

practice: Choose a single line and give it the whole sit.

If you pray, take a line you already know, say "Serve the LORD with gladness," and repeat it slowly on the out-breath, quieter each time, until it is almost only breath; if you don't, hum one simple tune with no words, over and over.
When your mind wanders, come back to the line or the tune; nobody is listening but you.
